paraphrase: Ajātasattu reports the answers of the six teachers: Pūraṇa Kassapa's doctrine that there is no evil or merit in deeds (non-action), Makkhali Gosāla's purification through wandering on in saṃsāra by fate, Ajita Kesakambalī's annihilationism (nothing survives death), Pakudha Kaccāyana's seven unmade bodies, the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta's fourfold restraint and Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta's evasion; each answered a question about fruits with something else.

Reported by opponents (a Buddhist text): these are the Sāmaññaphala's accounts of the six teachers, not their own words; the six teachers belong to U33.

paraphrase: Pūraṇa Kassapa, asked for a visible fruit of the ascetic life, says: one who acts or makes others act — mutilating, tormenting, killing, stealing, housebreaking, robbing, committing adultery, lying — does no evil. Were one to make all living beings on earth into one heap of flesh with a razor-edged wheel, no evil would come of it; killing on the south bank of the Ganges brings no evil, giving and sacrificing on the north bank brings no merit; there is no merit from giving, self-control, restraint or truthful speech. The king reports this as a doctrine of non-action (akiriya).

paraphrase: Six ministers each recommend a teacher to King Ajātasattu with the same praise: he leads an order and a community and tutors a community, is well known and famous, a ford-maker (titthakara) esteemed by many, long gone forth, advanced in years. The six are Pūraṇa Kassapa, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambalī, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta and Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.

paraphrase: Makkhali Gosāla says: there is no cause or condition for the defilement of beings or for their purification; there is no doing by oneself or by another, no human doing, no power, no energy, no human strength or vigour. All beings, all living things, all creatures, all souls are without control, power or energy; transformed by destiny, circumstance and nature (niyati-saṅgati-bhāva-pariṇatā), they experience pleasure and pain in the six classes (abhijāti). There is no ripening of unripe karma or wearing out of ripe karma by conduct, vows, austerity or the holy life; pleasure and pain are measured out as with a measure and saṃsāra is fixed in its limits, with no increase or decrease. As a ball of string, thrown, runs out unwinding, so fool and wise alike, having run and wandered through saṃsāra, will make an end of suffering. The king calls this 'purification through transmigration' (saṃsāra-suddhi).

paraphrase: Makkhali's enumerations: there are 1,400,000 principal kinds of birth, and 6,000 and 600; 500 kinds of karma, and five and three, full karma and half karma; 62 paths, 62 intermediate aeons, six classes of birth, eight stages of a person, 4,900 kinds of Ājīvaka and 4,900 kinds of wanderer, 4,900 abodes of nāgas, 2,000 faculties, 3,000 hells, 36 dust-realms, seven sentient and seven insentient wombs, seven knot-born wombs, seven gods, seven humans, seven goblins, seven lakes, seven and seven hundred knots, seven and seven hundred precipices, seven and seven hundred dreams, and 8,400,000 great aeons, through which fool and wise alike transmigrate and make an end of suffering.

paraphrase: Ajita Kesakambalī says: there is no gift, no sacrifice, no offering, no fruit or result of good and bad deeds, no this world, no other world, no mother, no father, no spontaneously born beings, no ascetics or brahmins in the world who, rightly practising, declare this world and the other from their own direct knowledge. This person is made of the four great elements; at death earth goes to the mass of earth, water to water, fire to fire, air to air, and the faculties pass into space. Four men with the bier as fifth carry the corpse; the footprints show as far as the burning-ground; the bones turn the colour of doves; offerings end in ashes. Giving is a doctrine of fools; the talk of those who assert existence is empty lying. Fool and wise alike are annihilated and destroyed at the breaking of the body and do not exist after death. The king calls this annihilation (uccheda).

paraphrase: Pakudha Kaccāyana says: there are seven bodies (kāya), unmade, not of a made kind, uncreated, without a creator, barren, steady as a mountain peak, standing firm as a pillar: the bodies of earth, water, fire and air, pleasure, pain, and the soul (jīva) as seventh. They do not move, change or harm one another and cannot cause one another pleasure or pain. There is no killer or one who causes killing, no hearer, no knower; one who cuts off a head with a sharp sword takes no one's life — the sword passes through the gap between the seven bodies. The king says he answered 'one thing by another'.

paraphrase: Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta says: 'If you ask me whether there is another world — if I thought there was, I would say so. But I do not say it is so, I do not say it is thus, I do not say it is otherwise, I do not say it is not, I do not say it is not not.' He answers the same way about there being no other world, both, and neither; about spontaneously born beings; about the fruit of good and bad deeds; and about whether the Tathāgata exists after death, does not, both, or neither. The king calls this evasion (vikkhepa).

paraphrase: Resorting to a secluded dwelling, sitting cross-legged with mindfulness established, he cleanses his mind of covetousness, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. The five hindrances are like a debt, a disease, a prison, slavery and a desert journey; their abandoning is like freedom from debt, health, release, emancipation and reaching safety — and on seeing them abandoned, gladness and joy arise.
